title: Parametric Motion Graphs
summary: Each graph node represents a continuous parameterized motion space constructed by blending aligned examples. Offline sampling finds acceptable transition regions between spaces and stores interpolation structures; runtime queries synthesize a clip and a compatible linear-blend transition rather than merely replaying a discrete edge.
limitations: Smooth parameter spaces and suitable examples are required. An edge cannot represent a source space containing any motion unable to transition to the target; restricting transitions can miss user targets. Linear blending is not a contact-force or dynamics certificate.
method: Each graph node represents a continuous parameterized motion space constructed by blending aligned examples. Offline sampling finds acceptable transition regions between spaces and stores interpolation structures; runtime queries synthesize a clip and a compatible linear-blend transition rather than merely replaying a discrete edge.
conditions: User-selected action and continuous controls such as travel curvature, punch target, duck height, platform height, and current character state. Action-specific functions translate joystick requests into graph parameters; feasible transition bounds can constrain the requested target.
data_split: Not applicable as a statistical train/test benchmark. Example-based authoring uses separate action collections; the general traversal graph organizes 256 examples and the boxing graph 275 examples into three nodes. No held-out subject or combination protocol is reported.
metrics: Transition similarity thresholds define acceptable edges. Reported engineering measurements include per-edge construction time (2–147 seconds), complete graph construction time, and storage below 50 KB; there is no modern FID or standardized quantitative naturalness score.
evaluation: Sections 5.1–5.2 demonstrate locomotion, mixed traversal, boxing, random walks, searches, and interactive control. The boxing graph has nine edges and takes about 7 minutes 40 seconds to construct; visual examples establish the demonstrated scope rather than measured unseen-composition generalization.
evidence_locator: §§3.1–3.3 (transition construction), §4 (runtime extraction), §§5.1–5.2 and Figures 6,10 (examples/timing), §6 (limitations).
full_text_version: Official primary PDF fetched 2026-11-19; file SHA-256 retained in private audit receipt.

title: PRISM: Per-unit Kinematic Motion Generation in a Structured Latent Manifold
summary: The inspected revision uses a causal temporal VAE with separate kinematic-unit latent tokens, a joint/time structured flow generator, kinematic-tree rotary positional encoding, and depth-dependent flow sampling. A clean-context mask provides prefix continuation and successive segment generation with one frozen generator.
limitations: The current PDF is retitled PRISM: Per-Unit Kinematic Motion Generation in a Structured Latent Manifold, so earlier streaming-title claims need revision alignment. SMPL body coverage excludes expressive hands/face; full object-conditioned interaction and dynamics are not evaluated.
publication_note: The inspected v4 PDF is retitled from "PRISM: Streaming Human Motion Generation with Per-Joint Latent Decomposition". The official BibTeX endpoint still returns that earlier title; this record transcribes the v4 title page and pins the citation to v4.
method: The inspected revision uses a causal temporal VAE with separate kinematic-unit latent tokens, a joint/time structured flow generator, kinematic-tree rotary positional encoding, and depth-dependent flow sampling. A clean-context mask provides prefix continuation and successive segment generation with one frozen generator.
conditions: Text and optional clean initial pose frames; long narratives are decomposed into ordered captions and durations shared across compared generators. The evaluated prefix lengths are 1, 5, and 9 frames. Arbitrary body-part or scattered-frame control is explicitly future work.
data_split: Trained on approximately 200,000 public MotionHub SMPL(-X) motion-text pairs; evaluates the HumanML3D split and FlowMDM BABEL protocol, plus 50 narratives in 10 categories containing 4–10 actions. Exact training-source group proportions are not reported in the inspected experimental description.
metrics: TMR-based R-Precision and MM-Distance measure semantic correspondence; FID measures feature-distribution differences; Diversity measures variability. BABEL transition FID evaluates boundaries. Shared-skeleton slide, float, and jitter errors probe kinematic artifacts; narrative rankings measure human preferences.
evaluation: Tables I–IV compare text generation, prefix conditioning, BABEL episodes, and reconstruction; matched 1D/2D, positional-encoding, and sampler ablations isolate design choices. Narrative outputs use frozen common plans and tie-aware ranking. This is paper-reported evidence, not an independent rerun.
evidence_locator: §III (causal kinematic-unit VAE, KU-FlowT, KT-RoPE, KAFS), §IV.A–G and Tables I–VIII; Appendix A shared TMR protocol and Appendix B narrative composition/user-study setup; §VI limitations.

title: Motion Mamba: Efficient and Long Sequence Motion Generation
summary: Motion Mamba replaces expensive denoising sequence operations with state-space blocks. Hierarchical Temporal Mamba varies temporal scan depth across the U-shaped network, while Bidirectional Spatial Mamba scans pose features in both directions to couple spatial channels and temporal dependencies.
limitations: The long-sequence experiment concerns single-description benchmark clips and cannot establish arbitrary multi-prompt temporal composition. Motion-feature scores and short generation latency do not establish contact correctness, scene compatibility, or full-body physical executability.
method: Motion Mamba replaces expensive denoising sequence operations with state-space blocks. Hierarchical Temporal Mamba varies temporal scan depth across the U-shaped network, while Bidirectional Spatial Mamba scans pose features in both directions to couple spatial channels and temporal dependencies.
conditions: Natural-language embeddings condition a diffusion motion generator; sequence duration follows benchmark generation settings. This is a text-to-motion backbone, without an explicit ordered action schedule, object mesh, scene map, or manipulation contact constraints as core input.
data_split: HumanML3D and KIT-ML follow the standard text-motion evaluation protocol. The paper does not restate exact train/validation/test proportions in §4.1. HumanML3D-LS selects original evaluation motions longer than 190 frames; this is a length slice, not a held-out action-combination split.
metrics: FID measures learned motion-feature distribution mismatch; R-Precision and MM-Distance measure text-motion alignment; Diversity and Multimodality measure overall and same-prompt variation. Average inference time measures latency on a single V100. Evaluations repeat 20 times with 95% confidence intervals.
evaluation: Tables 1–2 benchmark HumanML3D and KIT-ML, Table 3 tests the long-sequence slice, and Table 4 ablates temporal scans, spatial scans, latent size, and depth. Qualitative examples and a user study supplement numerical and speed comparisons.
evidence_locator: §3 and Figure 2 (HTM/BSM architecture), §§4.1–4.5, Tables 1–4, Figure 4 (V100 latency).

title: DiffCollage: Parallel Generation of Large Content with Diffusion Models
summary: DiffCollage represents large content through a factor graph of overlapping smaller regions. It combines local diffusion scores with overlap corrections to approximate a global score, allowing the regions to denoise concurrently. The same construction is applied to images and long human motion.
limitations: The factorization approximates the full distribution and depends on informative overlaps. Cropped feature metrics do not prove global ordering, distant consistency, collision freedom, or valid hand-object contact. The motion results should remain distinct from its stronger image-generation evaluation coverage.
method: DiffCollage represents large content through a factor graph of overlapping smaller regions. It combines local diffusion scores with overlap corrections to approximate a global score, allowing the regions to denoise concurrently. The same construction is applied to images and long human motion.
conditions: Pretrained short-content diffusion models and a chosen factor graph; motion factors may carry different text prompts. Overlap structure determines how local constraints communicate, while optional inpainting conditions preserve specified content. It is a sampling composition method rather than a new motion-capture dataset.
data_split: Motion experiments use the HumanML3D test set with an existing short-motion model. Long outputs are 24 seconds, approximately four times average training duration. Exact source-model train/validation proportions are not restated; image experiments additionally use internal landscapes, LHQ, and LSUN Tower.
metrics: R-Precision and multimodal distance assess text-motion alignment, FID measures distribution mismatch, and Diversity measures variability. Long-motion evaluation randomly crops generated sequences for short-motion evaluators, so its scores characterize local windows rather than complete narrative correctness.
evaluation: §5.2 and Table 3 compare parallel factor-graph generation with naive long denoising and autoregressive replacement/reconstruction. Multiple-action demonstrations provide qualitative prompt composition; image experiments additionally test panorama generation, inpainting, and latency scaling.
evidence_locator: §§3–4 (factor graphs and score assembly), §5.2, Table 3 and motion-composition examples; appendix implementation details.

title: TEACH: Temporal Action Composition for 3D Humans
summary: TEACH extends a text-motion variational Transformer with past-motion conditioning: it generates all frames of one action non-autoregressively, then conditions the next action on a short history. Training on adjacent action pairs teaches continuity; alignment and spherical interpolation further smooth transitions.
limitations: Pairwise BABEL supervision and validation-set reporting limit claims about unseen independent recordings and new action combinations. Autoregressive rollout can accumulate errors, while interpolation does not establish scene feasibility or contact-rich manipulation. Position-based comparison to one reference underestimates valid alternative realizations.
method: TEACH extends a text-motion variational Transformer with past-motion conditioning: it generates all frames of one action non-autoregressively, then conditions the next action on a short history. Training on adjacent action pairs teaches continuity; alignment and spherical interpolation further smooth transitions.
conditions: An ordered list of action descriptions, individual action durations, and the previous generated action tail. The main configuration uses five past frames. The model generates body motion and root displacement, without receiving manipulated object meshes or object-state trajectories.
evaluation: Table 1 compares independent, jointly generated, and past-conditioned action pairs; Table 2 tests alignment/interpolation and transition distances; Table 3 varies past-context length. Qualitative longer chains test repeated action-level rollout beyond pairwise training.
data_split: Uses original BABEL training/validation splits with approximately 23,400 training and 5,700 validation action pairs at 30 fps. Results are reported on validation because BABEL test data were unavailable; references to test pairs in some captions should not be mistaken for a public test evaluation.
metrics: Average Positional Error (APE) and Average Variational Error (AVE) compare root, trajectory, local, and global joint behavior with reference motion. Transition distance measures the joint-position gap between consecutive actions, both before and after alignment, exposing boundary discontinuity.
evidence_locator: §3 (hierarchical variational architecture), §§4.1–4.6, Tables 1–3; appendix D.1 explicitly states original splits and validation reporting.

title: CoMA: Compositional Human Motion Generation with Multi-modal Agents
summary: CoMA combines GPT-4o text recaptioning and temporal/body-part decomposition, a spatially aware masked generator (SPAM), trajectory editing, motion captioning, and visual self-correction. Four part-specific codebooks feed a shared whole-body decoder; factorized spatial and temporal attention coordinates the generated token streams.
limitations: Large-model calls, recaptioning, and rendered self-critique add cost and dependencies. Synthetic fine-grained language and complex-split construction affect comparability. Visual agreement and retrieval scores do not certify motion preservation, collision freedom, or interaction physics.
year_basis: First public preprint 2024; later venue not independently checked in this intake.
publication_note: AAAI 40(11), 9206–9214; DOI 10.1609/aaai.v40i11.37878. Published author list differs from the arXiv record; bibliography below cites the arXiv version. First public preprint 2024; later venue not independently checked in this intake.
method: CoMA combines GPT-4o text recaptioning and temporal/body-part decomposition, a spatially aware masked generator (SPAM), trajectory editing, motion captioning, and visual self-correction. Four part-specific codebooks feed a shared whole-body decoder; factorized spatial and temporal attention coordinates the generated token streams.
conditions: Natural-language requests and optional source motion or local edits. Agents transform rich prompts into shorter base-generation and part-edit instructions; rendered motions support visual critique. The complete agent system and its standalone SPAM generator are different evaluation objects.
data_split: Standard HumanML3D counts are 23,384 train, 1,460 validation, and 4,384 test samples. Appendix A separately constructs a complex-motion split of 20,108/2,932/2,172 samples, placing complex motions in test. These sample counts should not be presented as unique original recordings.
metrics: R-Precision and MM-Distance measure semantic alignment; FID and Multimodality characterize distribution and prompt diversity. Captioning uses BLEU, ROUGE, CIDEr, and BERTScore. Motion Alignment Score compares rendered-video and text embeddings; user studies judge rich-prompt fidelity and quality.
evaluation: Tables 2–3 primarily benchmark SPAM on standard and fine-grained descriptions; Table 4 evaluates captioning and Tables 5–7 test architecture and complex motions. The complete agent pipeline is evaluated with a 54-participant user study rather than assumed identical to SPAM benchmark scores.
evidence_locator: §§3–4 (agents and SPAM), §5 and Tables 2–6; appendix A (complex split/Table 7), B (54-participant study), F.4 (MAS).

title: MotionLab: Unified Human Motion Generation and Editing via the Motion-Condition-Motion Paradigm
summary: MotionLab formulates tasks as source motion, condition, and target motion. Its rectified-flow MotionFlow Transformer provides modality-specific paths with joint attention, aligned rotary position encoding, and task instruction modulation. Staged multitask training introduces modalities and tasks while replaying previous tasks.
limitations: Multitask breadth does not imply equal supervision or unseen-combination generalization. MotionFix target retrieval and recognizer-based style scores provide partial proxies for edit correctness. Body-only representation and foot-skating metrics do not validate detailed hand-object interactions or scene dynamics.
method: MotionLab formulates tasks as source motion, condition, and target motion. Its rectified-flow MotionFlow Transformer provides modality-specific paths with joint attention, aligned rotary position encoding, and task instruction modulation. Staged multitask training introduces modalities and tasks while replaying previous tasks.
conditions: Task instruction plus text, optional source motion, joint trajectories, temporal keyframes, or style reference. Generation uses an empty source; editing transforms a supplied source. Future full trajectories are task-specific controls, not evidence of unconstrained text-only generation.
data_split: Uses HumanML3D for text generation, trajectories, in-betweening, and style transfer, and MotionFix for editing. The inspected experimental setup names the datasets but does not restate exact split proportions or independent subject/recording grouping. All motions are retargeted to a common 22-joint, 20-fps representation.
metrics: FID, Diversity, R-Precision, and MM-Distance assess generation distributions/alignment; foot skating probes plausibility; AITS measures latency. Average Error measures keyframe/trajectory deviation, AvgR editing retrieval, SRA/CRA style/content recognition, and TSI source-trajectory preservation.
evaluation: Section 6 compares six tasks with specialist baselines and ablates instruction modulation, modality paths, aligned positions, and training stages. Main Tables 3–5 cover generation and editing, with in-between/style details in supplements. Timing is recomputed on one RTX 4090D.
evidence_locator: §4 (MCM task definitions), §5 and Figure 2 (MFT/training), §6 setup and metrics, Tables 3–9; supplementary in-between and style experiments.

title: MotionFix: Text-Driven 3D Human Motion Editing
summary: MotionFix mines semantically related source/target motion pairs with a retrieval model and collects human instructions describing the change. TMED learns conditional diffusion over the target using separate source-motion and text encodings, with independently dropped conditions enabling dual-condition classifier-free guidance.
limitations: One valid target is not the unique correct realization of an instruction, and embedding retrieval does not separately guarantee preservation of every unchanged detail. Random triplet splitting should not be read as independent-person generalization. No mesh-conditioned interaction or dynamics benchmark is claimed.
method: MotionFix mines semantically related source/target motion pairs with a retrieval model and collects human instructions describing the change. TMED learns conditional diffusion over the target using separate source-motion and text encodings, with independently dropped conditions enabling dual-condition classifier-free guidance.
conditions: A complete source motion and natural-language editing instruction; source and target can have different durations. The model learns edit relationships from explicit triplets rather than treating a new action description as equivalent to an instruction about a supplied motion.
data_split: The dataset contains 6,730 triplets and is randomly partitioned into 5,387 training, 330 validation, and 1,013 test triplets, described as 80/5/15%. The paper specifies triplet-level random splitting; it does not claim a cross-subject or source-recording-disjoint evaluation.
metrics: Motion-to-motion retrieval ranks the reference target against candidates using learned embeddings; top-K recall and average rank assess target proximity. The rank of the source indicates how much the output changes, but high source similarity alone is not successful editing.
evaluation: Section 5 compares TMED with text-motion-only baselines, body-part inpainting, and source initialization approaches. Data-size and condition-guidance ablations examine the value of paired editing supervision; qualitative edits show changed speed, direction, posture, or repetition.
evidence_locator: §3 (pair mining/annotation and 5387/330/1013 partition), §4 (TMED and guidance), §§5.1–5.3 (retrieval protocol, comparisons, ablations).

title: MotionCLIP: Exposing Human Motion Generation to CLIP Space
summary: MotionCLIP trains a Transformer motion autoencoder whose latent code aligns with frozen CLIP text and rendered-image embeddings. Reconstruction and geometric losses retain motion information, while semantic alignment supports text-driven decoding, interpolation, action arithmetic, and style changes directly in the learned latent space.
limitations: The model struggles with directional language and detailed controls. CLIP alignment inherits image/text biases and may map unfamiliar descriptions to nearby known actions. Latent addition provides no strict source-preservation, temporal ordering, contact, or physical-validity guarantee.
method: MotionCLIP trains a Transformer motion autoencoder whose latent code aligns with frozen CLIP text and rendered-image embeddings. Reconstruction and geometric losses retain motion information, while semantic alignment supports text-driven decoding, interpolation, action arithmetic, and style changes directly in the learned latent space.
conditions: Text or image embeddings can drive decoding; existing motions provide codes for editing and interpolation. Text labels and rendered frames supervise alignment during training. Semantic latent arithmetic differs from explicit per-joint constraints or a scheduled chain of independently specified actions.
data_split: Training uses BABEL/AMASS at 30 fps, cut into 60-frame sequences whose action labels are concatenated; recognition follows the BABEL-60 benchmark. Exact train/test counts and percentages are not restated in the inspected setup. Semantic editing demonstrations do not constitute a held-out combination split.
metrics: Top-1 and Top-5 action-recognition accuracy measure class information on BABEL-60. Pairwise user preference measures text-driven action generation and style transfer; architecture/loss ablations test semantic representation. No FID-based generation leaderboard is reported here, and these measures do not directly quantify edit locality.
evaluation: Section 4 tests text-to-motion, action recognition/generation, interpolation, and style editing. Comparing text-only versus image/text alignment and reconstruction components helps separate CLIP alignment effects. Abstract prompts and pop-culture examples demonstrate qualitative semantic transfer rather than verified object interaction.
evidence_locator: §3 and Figures 2–3 (alignment/autoencoder), §4 application experiments and ablations; concluding discussion of directional limitations; supplementary experimental settings.

title: T2M-GPT: Generating Human Motion from Textual Descriptions with Discrete Representations
summary: T2M-GPT first trains a convolutional VQ-VAE to compress motion into discrete indices, using exponential-moving-average code updates and code reset. A text-conditioned causal Transformer predicts indices autoregressively; deliberately corrupted input indices reduce the discrepancy between teacher-forced training and sampled inference.
limitations: Token quantization limits fine-grained edit resolution and can introduce jitter; autoregressive errors remain possible despite corruption training. A strong short-text benchmark result does not establish long ordered composition, unseen object manipulation, or physically executable control.
method: T2M-GPT first trains a convolutional VQ-VAE to compress motion into discrete indices, using exponential-moving-average code updates and code reset. A text-conditioned causal Transformer predicts indices autoregressively; deliberately corrupted input indices reduce the discrepancy between teacher-forced training and sampled inference.
conditions: A CLIP text embedding initializes generation; sampled motion-code tokens become subsequent context and a learned end token terminates output. No object geometry, scene map, or explicit body-part schedule is required in its principal text-to-motion task.
data_split: HumanML3D and KIT-ML each use 80% training, 5% validation, and 15% test motions following the cited benchmark protocol. Model selection minimizes validation FID; test results are then reported. HumanML3D is processed at 20 fps and KIT-ML at 12.5 fps.
metrics: R-Precision and MM-Distance measure text-motion correspondence in pretrained feature spaces; FID measures generated/reference distribution mismatch; Diversity measures across-sample variation and Multimodality variation for one prompt. Reconstruction FID and retrieval quantify tokenizer quality separately from full generation.
evaluation: Tables 1–2 compare benchmark generation, and Table 3 tests EMA/code-reset combinations. Appendix ablations vary corruption rate, architecture, losses, and dataset amount. Metrics are repeated 20 times with confidence intervals; length-conditioned competitors are marked separately.
evidence_locator: §§3.1–3.2 (VQ-VAE/GPT), §4.1 (80/5/15 protocols), Tables 1–3; appendix C (corruption), E (metrics), G (limitations).

title: Human Motion Diffusion Model
summary: MDM uses a classifier-free Transformer diffusion model predicting clean motion rather than noise, making position, velocity, and foot-contact losses available directly. It supports text-, action-, and unconditional generation; clamping known regions during denoising enables temporal in-betweening and body-part editing.
limitations: Foot-contact losses improve selected visible artifacts but do not establish dynamical validity. Inpainting is primarily demonstrated qualitatively, and benchmark scores do not certify edit preservation or action ordering. Expensive iterative diffusion and fixed evaluator assumptions affect practical comparisons.
method: MDM uses a classifier-free Transformer diffusion model predicting clean motion rather than noise, making position, velocity, and foot-contact losses available directly. It supports text-, action-, and unconditional generation; clamping known regions during denoising enables temporal in-betweening and body-part editing.
conditions: Text embeddings, action labels, or no condition depending on the trained model. Editing supplies observed frames or joints. Main text benchmarks use reference motion lengths, an important difference from autonomous length prediction and free-form narrative planning.
data_split: HumanML3D/KIT follow benchmark splits, with exact text-motion proportions not restated in the inspected setup. UESTC uses the cross-subject protocol and HumanAct12 the provided sequences. Main text results use 20 evaluations; Multimodality uses five.
metrics: R-Precision/MM-Distance assess text alignment, FID feature-distribution mismatch, Diversity overall variation, and Multimodality same-condition variation. Action tasks add recognition accuracy; unconditional evaluation adds KID and precision/recall. User comparisons supplement learned-feature proxies.
evaluation: Tables 1–2 evaluate text generation, Tables 3–4 action generation, and Table 5 unconditional generation; §5.1 demonstrates inpainting. Backbone and guidance sweeps are reported. Crucially, text experiments do not apply geometric losses because joints/contact are explicit in the representation.
evidence_locator: §3 and Equations 2–5 (clean prediction/geometric losses), §§4.1–4.2, Tables 1–5, §5.1 (editing), Figure 4 (guidance/user study).

title: TEMOS: Generating diverse human motions from textual descriptions
summary: TEMOS learns paired variational Transformer encoders for text and motion with a shared decoder. Reconstruction, embedding-similarity, Gaussian-prior, and cross-modal distribution losses align their latent distributions; sampling from the text latent generates multiple plausible motions for a description.
limitations: One-reference coordinate errors penalize diverse valid outputs, while oracle best-of-ten overstates a deployable single sample. KIT is dominated by limited movement categories. The model lacks detailed object/contact inputs, and a shared semantic latent does not itself prove compositional generalization.
method: TEMOS learns paired variational Transformer encoders for text and motion with a shared decoder. Reconstruction, embedding-similarity, Gaussian-prior, and cross-modal distribution losses align their latent distributions; sampling from the text latent generates multiple plausible motions for a description.
conditions: Natural language and requested duration, implemented through decoder positional encodings. A frozen DistilBERT supplies language features. Generation requires no initial ground-truth pose, unlike several compared earlier methods, and does not model manipulated object geometry.
data_split: KIT protocol extracts 1,784 training, 566 validation, and 587 test motions; common comparison uses 520 test sequences available from a baseline. KIT-SMPL maps to 2,888 annotated AMASS sequences. This differs from later 80/5/15 KIT protocols and should not be pooled blindly.
metrics: Average Positional Error (APE) and Average Variance Error (AVE) compare root, trajectory, local, and global joint coordinates after canonicalization. Single-random, latent-mean, average-of-ten, and best-of-ten sampling results have distinct interpretations; best-of-ten uses reference-based selection.
evaluation: Table 1 compares earlier text-motion systems; Table 2 separates deterministic and variational sampling; Tables 3–4 ablate architecture/losses and frozen language features. Appendix C documents metric implementation corrections and human-study details, useful for fair reproduction.
evidence_locator: §3 architecture/losses, §4.1 exact KIT counts and 520-sequence subset, Tables 1–4; appendices A.5 and C (sampling and metric caveats).

title: Unpaired Motion Style Transfer from Video to Animation
summary: The style-transfer network separates temporally varying motion content from a temporally invariant style code. A convolutional decoder uses adaptive instance normalization to inject style, with reconstruction, adversarial, and latent constraints; aligned 2D/3D style embeddings allow style extraction from video poses.
limitations: Small style vocabularies can overfit: unseen-style generalization improves with the larger collection. Style/content separation is learned rather than formally identifiable, and temporal convolutions do not guarantee contact preservation. The task concerns appearance of motion, not semantic task ordering or object manipulation.
method: The style-transfer network separates temporally varying motion content from a temporally invariant style code. A convolutional decoder uses adaptive instance normalization to inject style, with reconstruction, adversarial, and latent constraints; aligned 2D/3D style embeddings allow style extraction from video poses.
conditions: A content motion and reference style from a 3D motion or estimated 2D joints in a short video. Training uses unpaired motions carrying style labels rather than paired same-content examples across every style. Output rotations can directly animate a character.
data_split: Two motion collections yield approximately 1,500 and 10,500 overlapping 32-frame clips; each has disjoint train/test samples with 10% held out. Separate experiments exclude an entire style to test unseen-style transfer. This clip split does not establish source-recording independence.
metrics: Human ratings measure realism, content preservation, and style transfer. PCA/t-SNE visualizations examine content/style organization and phase behavior. Table 1 reports preference and realism ratios; the paper does not introduce FID-based standardized text-motion evaluation.
evaluation: Section 5 compares against Holden-style transfer and other baselines, tests seen/unseen styles, style interpolation, video-derived style, and loss/representation ablations. User questions distinguish whether the content was retained from whether the target style was transferred.
evidence_locator: §§3–4 (content/style encoders, AdaIN and training collections), §5 and Table 1; unseen-style and content-code analyses in Figures 5–8.

title: Harnessing Coupled Stream Completion For Human-Object Interaction Modeling
summary: TRACE separates body, hand, and object motion through aligned temporal VAEs, then couples all latent streams with a joint flow network whose velocity predictions depend on the complete interaction state. Decoded estimates receive contact, object-frame anchoring, and timing supervision; a language branch also supports interaction understanding.
limitations: Interaction metrics depend on thresholded proxy contacts and fitted body geometry. Coupled latent responses and improved feature scores do not prove force consistency, continuous collision freedom, or generalization to unseen data sources. All numerical findings here are inspected paper claims rather than reproduced results.
method: TRACE separates body, hand, and object motion through aligned temporal VAEs, then couples all latent streams with a joint flow network whose velocity predictions depend on the complete interaction state. Decoded estimates receive contact, object-frame anchoring, and timing supervision; a language branch also supports interaction understanding.
conditions: Text, object geometry encoded by 1,024-point BPS, and optional observed streams for completion. The architecture predicts continuous body/hand/object states jointly; future object motion is not assumed supplied for ordinary text-to-HOI generation.
data_split: Uses the official InterAct train/test partition, converting mixed SMPL-H/SMPL-X data consistently to SMPL-H. The inspected experimental section does not report exact partition proportions or assert cross-dataset ancestor-disjointness. Generation, completion, and understanding share preprocessing and evaluators.
metrics: R-Precision/MM-Distance assess language alignment; FID/Diversity distribution and variation. Foot Skating Ratio, penetration ratio, contact ratio, and contact precision/recall/F1 probe geometric interaction. Understanding adds BLEU-1/4, ROUGE, CIDEr, and BERTScore for generated descriptions.
evaluation: Section 4 compares retrained HOI-Diff and other HOI baselines, completion variants, and language-generation baselines under the common protocol. Twenty repeated evaluations report means and 95% confidence intervals; coupled-flow and geometric-supervision ablations test the proposed mechanisms.
evidence_locator: §3 (split VAE, coupled flow, geometric objectives), §4 setup/metrics and Tables 1–2; completion and coupling ablations in experimental subsections.

title: InteractMove: Text-Controlled Human-Object Interaction Generation in 3D Scenes with Movable Objects
summary: InterActMove introduces text-conditioned joint human/object generation in scenes with movable objects. AGCA first grounds the referenced object, predicts hand-object affordances, and denoises interaction with local scene features. Contact/penetration losses and test-time penetration guidance encourage target interaction and scene compatibility.
limitations: Grounding mistakes propagate through the pipeline. Learned realism and sampled geometric collision scores are incomplete physical proxies. Exact partition details remain a reporting gap, and scene augmentation must not be counted as independent captured interaction. No force-based certification is established.
method: InterActMove introduces text-conditioned joint human/object generation in scenes with movable objects. AGCA first grounds the referenced object, predicts hand-object affordances, and denoises interaction with local scene features. Contact/penetration losses and test-time penetration guidance encourage target interaction and scene compatibility.
conditions: Free-form text and a 3D scene containing separate object point clouds; a pretrained grounding module selects the target instance. Object geometry, affordance features, and surrounding local geometry condition generated body motion and object trajectories.
data_split: The constructed dataset contains 618 sequences, 71 objects, 21 scenes, and approximately 2.2 million frames. Evaluation also uses the movable-object subset of TRUMANS. Exact train/test proportions and subject/recording split units are not reported in the inspected main experiment description.
metrics: Goal Distance averages minimum human-object surface distance; Multimodality measures L2 variation for a fixed prompt/scene. Physical Realism is a pretrained frame classifier score, not a dynamics calculation. Non-collision Score measures the proportion of frames without detected penetration.
evaluation: Tables 2–3 compare interaction generation on the new dataset and TRUMANS subset; ablations remove grounding, affordance, local scene modeling, and collision-aware components. Scene/object augmentation adjusts object placement and interaction trajectories before diffusion-based refinement.
evidence_locator: §3 and Table 1 (dataset/augmentation), §§4.1–4.5 (AGCA), §5.1 metric definitions, Tables 2–4 (comparisons and ablations).

title: Object Motion Guided Human Motion Synthesis
summary: OMOMO uses two diffusion stages: object geometry and motion first predict hand positions, then hand positions guide full-body motion synthesis. Geometry-aware hand correction enforces object-relative contact before body generation; captured SMPL-X body/object trajectories provide supervision.
limitations: Conditioning on the complete object trajectory makes this adjacent to initial-state-conditioned HOI generation. Hand constraints are heuristic and no full-body optimization eliminates all artifacts. Held-out objects are only five specified instances; this does not establish arbitrary scene or manipulation transfer.
method: OMOMO uses two diffusion stages: object geometry and motion first predict hand positions, then hand positions guide full-body motion synthesis. Geometry-aware hand correction enforces object-relative contact before body generation; captured SMPL-X body/object trajectories provide supervision.
conditions: A known object mesh and its full motion trajectory condition human motion. Future object poses are inputs in this reconstruction/animation setting, so results must not be described as jointly generating object trajectories from only initial object state.
data_split: The dataset has 17 subjects and 15 objects. Fifteen subjects train and two test; one evaluation shares all 15 objects, while another uses 10 training and five unseen test objects. Subject and object generalization therefore have explicitly different settings.
metrics: Hand JPE, MPJPE, and MPVPE compare hand/body joints and mesh vertices; root translation/orientation errors measure global alignment. Collision percentage, foot sliding, and contact precision/recall/F1 probe geometric plausibility. Best-of-multiple sampling and subjective comparisons require distinct interpretation.
evaluation: Tables 2–3 compare GOAL, single-stage diffusion, constraint-free OMOMO, and the full system under both object partitions. User preferences and a smartphone-mounted object-tracking application supplement reference errors. The paper acknowledges remaining penetration despite visually improved hand contact.
evidence_locator: §3 (two-stage generation and hand correction), §4/Table 1 (capture), §5.1 (15/2 subjects, 10/5 objects and metrics), Tables 2–3, §6 application.

title: SAGA: Stochastic Whole-Body Grasping with Contact
summary: SAGA combines WholeGrasp-VAE, which samples full-body grasp poses and contacts around an object, with MotionFill-VAE, which fills a transition from an initial body state to the sampled grasp. Marker-based optimization then fits SMPL-X and improves contact and collision behavior.
limitations: Optimization and contact thresholds add sensitivity and runtime. End-grasp quality does not guarantee every intermediate frame is collision-free or dynamically feasible; a stationary target and short approach window limit long manipulation claims. GRAB-derived grouping must preserve object and source ancestry.
method: SAGA combines WholeGrasp-VAE, which samples full-body grasp poses and contacts around an object, with MotionFill-VAE, which fills a transition from an initial body state to the sampled grasp. Marker-based optimization then fits SMPL-X and improves contact and collision behavior.
conditions: A target object mesh and starting human state; the method samples an ending whole-body grasp and the intervening motion. It does not require an entire future object path, but its primary interaction is approaching and grasping a stationary target rather than unrestricted long manipulation.
data_split: GRAB right-hand grasps follow the GrabNet object partition: 41 training, four validation, six test objects. MotionFill uses 62-frame approach-to-grasp clips at 30 fps; AMASS supplies 61-frame pretraining clips. HO3D objects test additional shape transfer without a stated statistical split ratio.
metrics: Contact Ratio measures proximity contact; interpenetration volume/depth quantify mesh intersections; APD measures diversity. Marker ADE compares deterministic predictions, with minimum error over 10 samples for stochastic motion. PSKL-J compares acceleration power spectra as a smoothness proxy.
evaluation: Tables 1–2 evaluate grasp sampling and optimization losses; motion experiments compare transition models and local/global completion components. Qualitative HO3D results assess unseen object geometries. Explicitly distinguish best-of-ten reference matching from a single deployed sample.
evidence_locator: §3 (WholeGrasp/MotionFill and optimizers), §4 experiments and Tables 1–2; supplementary training-data section naming 41/4/6 objects and motion metrics.

title: Diffusion-based Generation, Optimization, and Planning in 3D Scenes
summary: SceneDiffuser unifies conditional diffusion, differentiable objective guidance, and planning. Scene/object point-cloud features condition denoising; gradients of collision, contact, or task costs steer samples at inference. The framework handles poses, motions, dexterous grasps, path planning, and robot motion planning with task-specific representations.
limitations: Differentiable surrogate costs and averaged frame scores do not ensure continuous collision freedom or stable dynamic manipulation. Human ratings still show substantial implausibility. Cross-task architectural reuse is not evidence of one joint controller handling every tested output type.
method: SceneDiffuser unifies conditional diffusion, differentiable objective guidance, and planning. Scene/object point-cloud features condition denoising; gradients of collision, contact, or task costs steer samples at inference. The framework handles poses, motions, dexterous grasps, path planning, and robot motion planning with task-specific representations.
conditions: 3D scene or object point clouds, optional start pose, and differentiable goals or constraints. The generated variable changes by task, so dexterous grasp and robot planning findings should not be merged into a single full-body language-conditioned manipulation claim.
data_split: PROX pose/motion evaluation uses roughly 53,000 training frames from eight scenes and held-out scenes following prior work; four test scenes support human ratings. MultiDex ShadowHand grasp evaluation uses 48 training and 10 unseen test objects. These are distinct task-specific partitions.
metrics: Human plausible rate, non-collision score, and contact score measure perceived/geometric validity; APD and standard deviation measure diversity. Grasp success is tested in physics under collision-depth settings. Planning experiments additionally report goal success and efficiency, rather than only motion-feature FID.
evaluation: Section 5 evaluates five tasks, with Tables 1–2 separating pose/motion and start-pose conditions, and Table 3 testing dexterous grasps. Guided and unguided sampling ablations isolate optimization effects; motion metrics average framewise pose scores.
evidence_locator: §4 (conditional denoising/objective guidance), §§5.2–5.6, Tables 1–3; §5.2 PROX split and §5.4 MultiDex 48/10-object protocol.

title: Stochastic Scene-Aware Motion Prediction
summary: SAMP combines an autoregressive conditional-VAE MotionNet, an object-conditioned GoalNet, and a path planner. GoalNet samples plausible contact positions/orientations; MotionNet predicts subsequent body state from prior state, local object geometry, target goals, and action information while the planner routes locomotion around obstacles.
limitations: The five-action vocabulary and furniture-centered capture constrain scope. Geometric collision and feature-distribution metrics are not force validation, and autoregressive rollout can drift. NSM comparisons use different supervision availability, which must remain visible rather than treated as perfectly matched training.
method: SAMP combines an autoregressive conditional-VAE MotionNet, an object-conditioned GoalNet, and a path planner. GoalNet samples plausible contact positions/orientations; MotionNet predicts subsequent body state from prior state, local object geometry, target goals, and action information while the planner routes locomotion around obstacles.
conditions: A scene, target object and action label, prior character motion, and interaction goals. Five modeled actions are idle, walk, run, sit, and lie down. Stochastic latent sampling supplies alternative styles; a global planner supports locomotion before the terminal interaction.
data_split: Uses newly captured interaction motions plus ShapeNet objects from sofa, L-shaped sofa, chair, armchair, and table categories. The main description does not specify a standard percentage or subject-disjoint train/test partition. Some baseline comparisons retrain SAMP on NSM training data for compatibility.
metrics: Diversity measures generated motion variation; execution time measures time to reach an action, with failures beyond three minutes marked infinite. Goal precision measures task accuracy and Fréchet distance compares generated/reference motions. Scene penetration is measured as the fraction of colliding frames.
evaluation: Section 5 tests diverse transitions, unseen furniture configurations, goals, and obstacle navigation. Tables 1–4 compare diversity, execution time, precision, and Fréchet distance; ablations remove GoalNet or path planning. Scene collision tests repeat randomized placements ten times.
evidence_locator: §3 (MotionNet/GoalNet/planner), §4 (motion and ShapeNet preparation), §§5.1–5.2, Tables 1–4 and Figure 6 (GoalNet ablation).

title: Learning to Generate Human-Human-Object Interactions from Textual Descriptions
summary: The method learns separate score-based priors for human-object and human-human configurations, then combines their scores during guided sampling. Consistency and collision constraints reconcile shared humans across factors, enabling a variable number of people around one object without paired multi-person training for every composition.
limitations: Composition of static pairwise priors does not ensure globally compatible dynamic cooperation. CLIP similarity and person-count success do not establish task completion. Random sample splitting and synthetic reconstruction can preserve correlated geometry or pose errors across evaluation data.
method: The method learns separate score-based priors for human-object and human-human configurations, then combines their scores during guided sampling. Consistency and collision constraints reconcile shared humans across factors, enabling a variable number of people around one object without paired multi-person training for every composition.
conditions: An object mesh, textual description, and desired participant count. Generated variables are body poses, scales, rotations, and translations in object/person-centered coordinates. This is static HHOI configuration generation, not continuous multi-person motion or temporal manipulation synthesis.
data_split: Combines CORE4D-derived samples, multiview captures, and synthetic image-derived samples across 19 object categories. After preprocessing, training/test samples are split 9:1. The appendix does not claim subject/recording-disjoint grouping; repeated person-reference transformations must not be counted as independent captures.
metrics: Body-pose FD and interpersonal-distance FD compare distributions; multiview CLIP Score assesses prompt similarity. Desired-person-count success tests 3–5 people. Human-human/object penetration ratios and selected hand/hip contact distances probe geometry, while user preferences judge realism and text coherence.
evaluation: Tables 1–2 compare dyadic and multi-human generation against adapted GenZI and depth-optimization baselines; physical metrics and qualitative failures supplement these scores. The real/synthetic data preparation and sample counts are detailed in appendix A.
evidence_locator: §§3.1–3.3 (HOI/HHI score composition), §5.1 metric definitions, Tables 1–2; appendix A.2–A.3 (9:1 split, sources/statistics).

title: HiPHI: A Large-Scale Benchmark for High-Precision Human Motion and Object-Interaction
summary: HiPHI organizes studio optical motion capture through FrameNet frames and lexical units, expanding motion seeds by direction, speed, amplitude, body-part participation, and object/contact factors. The release provides BVH motion plus aligned mesh/object trajectories for a stricter interaction subset and benchmarks humanoid tracking.
limitations: Only single-person studio motion is captured; forces and tactile signals are not directly measured. Sparse centerline geometry and 20-cm near-surface thresholds are not dense-mesh contact certification. Hardware demonstrations cannot establish all 617.5 hours are executable or every asset is already released.
method: HiPHI organizes studio optical motion capture through FrameNet frames and lexical units, expanding motion seeds by direction, speed, amplitude, body-part participation, and object/contact factors. The release provides BVH motion plus aligned mesh/object trajectories for a stricter interaction subset and benchmarks humanoid tracking.
conditions: This is a dataset/benchmark rather than a text-to-motion generator. Semantic Frame-LU indices, actor metadata, human kinematics, and object state support downstream retrieval and control; recorded future trajectories are supervision, not initial-state-only generative inputs.
data_split: Reports 617.5 hours from 132 performers and 214 Frame-LUs, including 245.7 object-state-aligned hours. No conventional train/validation/test proportions or held-out-subject generation split is reported in the inspected benchmark. Tracking comparisons use common retargeting/control settings, not an independent composition test.
metrics: Projected-grid occupancy, effective occupancy, and long-tail share measure motion-space coverage. Jerk, acceleration, below-ground depth, floating share, and support drift probe kinematics; sparse-skeleton non-conflict and near-surface grounding assess interaction geometry. Tracking/recovery and hardware demonstrations assess downstream usability.
evaluation: Section 5 compares equal-size coverage samples, motion quality, and Unitree G1 tracking against existing datasets; appendix analyses vary projection and grid settings. Table 2 explicitly separates body precision and object geometry; real hardware examples cover locomotion and object-related actions.
evidence_locator: §§3–4 (FrameNet construction/capture), §§5.1–5.4 and Tables 1–2, Figures 7–8; §7 limitations; appendices B/E geometry and robustness details.

title: Go to Zero: Towards Zero-shot Motion Generation with Million-scale Data
summary: MotionMillion builds web-video motion/text data through shot detection, person tracking, confidence/transition filtering, world-grounded human reconstruction, and jitter filtering. GPT-4o captions are rewritten by Llama for linguistic diversity. A wavelet-assisted finite-scalar-quantization tokenizer feeds scalable text-conditioned autoregressive Transformers.
limitations: Web-video reconstruction and automatic captions introduce pseudo-label and semantic errors. More captions do not create independent captured motions. Filtering by smoothness can suppress legitimate dynamics, and unreported source-level partitioning limits leakage assessment. No object-conditioned manipulation guarantee is established.
method: MotionMillion builds web-video motion/text data through shot detection, person tracking, confidence/transition filtering, world-grounded human reconstruction, and jitter filtering. GPT-4o captions are rewritten by Llama for linguistic diversity. A wavelet-assisted finite-scalar-quantization tokenizer feeds scalable text-conditioned autoregressive Transformers.
conditions: Text descriptions condition body-motion generation, with T5-XL language features and discrete motion tokens. The corpus contains reconstructed human motion and expanded captions, not measured object trajectories or contact forces. Caption rewrites share the same motion identity.
data_split: The paper reports about two million motions and over 2,000 hours; training and evaluation sets are used for reconstruction and generation, but exact split proportions and video/performer grouping are not reported in the inspected setup. HumanML3D and Motion-X are also used for cross-dataset reconstruction.
metrics: MPJPE measures motion-tokenizer reconstruction; mean/max acceleration and jerk quantify temporal roughness. FID and R@1/2/3 assess generation distribution and text retrieval; MotionMillion-Eval uses human text-alignment, smoothness, and plausibility scores on 126 prompts. These metrics have differing supervision assumptions.
evaluation: Section 5 tests tokenizer transfer across MotionUnion-related data, wavelet ablation, model scaling, and long text-conditioned sequences. Tables 2–3 separate reconstruction accuracy and smoothing, while Table 4 compares model sizes on MotionMillion; additional criteria appear in the supplement.
evidence_locator: §3 data pipeline, §§4.2–4.3 (wavelet FSQ/scaled Transformer), §§5.1–5.3 and Tables 2–4; appendix §§8–9 distribution and scoring criteria.

title: Motion-X: A Large-scale 3D Expressive Whole-body Human Motion Dataset
summary: Motion-X constructs expressive SMPL-X body/hand/face motion with a progressive whole-body annotation pipeline and semantic plus pose text. The method combines 2D keypoints, learning-based fitting, and text annotation, then evaluates whether the resulting corpus improves text-driven motion generation and whole-body mesh recovery.
limitations: Automatic fits are pseudo-ground truth and can retain occlusion/depth errors. Random motion partitions do not independently demonstrate source-actor generalization. Expressive hand/face coverage and feature improvements do not establish object contact accuracy or physically executable manipulation.
method: Motion-X constructs expressive SMPL-X body/hand/face motion with a progressive whole-body annotation pipeline and semantic plus pose text. The method combines 2D keypoints, learning-based fitting, and text annotation, then evaluates whether the resulting corpus improves text-driven motion generation and whole-body mesh recovery.
conditions: The dataset supplies RGB observations, pseudo/real fitted whole-body parameters, semantic sequence text, and detailed body/face descriptions. Text-motion benchmarks condition generation on captions; this is not inherently a human-object interaction dataset with tracked movable object states.
data_split: Motion-X is randomly divided into 80% training, 5% validation, and 15% test. The reported unit is dataset motions; no subject- or original-video-disjoint guarantee is stated. Additional annotation-pipeline evaluation uses COCO-WholeBody and EHF, while downstream reconstruction tests EHF/AGORA.
metrics: 2D AP/AR assess keypoints; MPVPE, PA-MPVPE, and PA-MPJPE assess 3D fitting. FID, R-Precision, MM-Distance, Diversity, and Multimodality assess motion generation via learned embeddings. Twenty runs are used except five for Multimodality.
evaluation: Tables 3–4 evaluate annotation quality and generation baselines; later tables compare HumanML3D training, body/face text additions, and downstream mesh recovery. MLD, MDM, MotionDiffuse, and T2M-GPT provide distinct benchmark baselines, not all diffusion architectures.
evidence_locator: §3 annotation pipeline, §4 dataset, §§5.1–5.3, Tables 3–7; §5.2 explicitly states 80/5/15 and repetition protocol; appendix metric definitions.

title: InterCap: Joint Markerless 3D Tracking of Humans and Objects in Interaction
summary: InterCap estimates jointly moving SMPL-X humans and rigid objects from synchronized multiview RGB-D observations. Segmentation, detected joints, object pose initialization, and temporally coupled optimization combine depth fitting, pose priors, contact encouragement, and collision constraints to reconstruct captured interactions without optical body markers.
limitations: Occlusion, depth noise, segmentation, and object initialization limit accuracy. Contact is inferred from fitted geometry and should not be treated as force sensing. Markerless capture improves accessibility but cannot establish exact dense contact or any text-conditioned compositional generation capability.
method: InterCap estimates jointly moving SMPL-X humans and rigid objects from synchronized multiview RGB-D observations. Segmentation, detected joints, object pose initialization, and temporally coupled optimization combine depth fitting, pose priors, contact encouragement, and collision constraints to reconstruct captured interactions without optical body markers.
conditions: Multiple calibrated RGB-D streams and known scanned object geometry. The method reconstructs observed interaction rather than generating new motion from text. Fitted body/object trajectories and proximity-derived contact are dataset outputs with their own reconstruction uncertainty.
data_split: The capture dataset contains multiple subjects and everyday object interactions; the reconstruction method is evaluated on captured sequences, not a learned text-generation split. A conventional training/validation/test percentage is not applicable to its main optimization experiment and is not reported as a generation benchmark.
metrics: Body/object vertex-to-segmented-point-cloud distances quantify observation fit. Mean penetration depth characterizes reconstructed contact frames; contact maps threshold closest human-object distances at 4.5 mm. Per-frame comparisons with the segmented depth observations assess fitting accuracy, separately from qualitative render inspection; no independent full-body ground-truth trajectory is assumed.
evaluation: Section 5 analyzes contact heatmaps, reconstruction errors, object/human alignment, and mesh penetration. Real data average vertex-to-cloud errors are 20.29 mm for bodies and 18.50 mm for objects; these are sensor-fit distances, not independent full-surface ground-truth errors.
evidence_locator: §3 InterCap optimization, §4 dataset/capture, §5 experiments (contact heatmaps, mesh penetration, fitting accuracy); §§3.3–3.4 depth fitting and manually annotated contact constraints.

title: GRAB: A Dataset of Whole-Body Human Grasping of Objects
summary: GRAB captures whole-body interaction with 51 objects using optical markers and individualized SMPL-X fitting. Proximity and mesh intersection analysis derive detailed body-object contact. GrabNet separately learns a coarse conditional VAE plus refinement network to synthesize right-hand grasps from object geometry.
limitations: Studio markers can influence contact and conceal touch regions; mesh proximity is not measured force. GrabNet evaluates right hands, while dataset breadth includes more body parts. Grasp-frame counts cannot substitute for independent actors or full continuous interactions in downstream splitting.
method: GRAB captures whole-body interaction with 51 objects using optical markers and individualized SMPL-X fitting. Proximity and mesh intersection analysis derive detailed body-object contact. GrabNet separately learns a coarse conditional VAE plus refinement network to synthesize right-hand grasps from object geometry.
conditions: Captured observations supply body, finger, face, and rigid object trajectories; GrabNet receives object shape/geometry to predict a hand grasp. Static grasp synthesis is distinct from generating a complete body/object manipulation sequence from text and initial state.
data_split: GrabNet holds out four validation and six test objects, leaving 41 for training; supplementary data counts are roughly 320k/31k/65k training/validation/test grasp samples. These are frames/grasps, not independent motion sequences. GRAB itself contains 1,334 sequences and approximately 1.62 million frames.
metrics: Closest-reference vertex distance measures grasp resemblance; contact comparisons assess similarity of contact patterns; AMT ratings score realism from one to five. Capture analyses measure contact prevalence and mesh penetration. MoSh++ synthetic fitting evaluation has separate subject/pose partitions.
evaluation: Table 2 evaluates six unseen test objects, comparing generated and recorded grasp ratings and nearest-reference geometry. Contact heatmaps and intent-specific statistics characterize use/pass/lift/off-hand interactions. Synthetic model-fitting tests should remain separate from GrabNet generalization results.
evidence_locator: §3/Table 1 (capture/contact/statistics), §4/Table 2 (GrabNet), supplementary S.8–S.9 (object partitions/evaluation), S.10 (marker bias).

title: MaskAdapt: Learning Flexible Motion Adaptation via Mask-Invariant Prior for Physics-Based Characters
summary: MaskAdapt learns an adversarial base policy with observation masks and a mask-invariant regularizer, then trains a residual adaptation policy controlling selected parts. The base preserves non-adapted behavior while residual rewards teach new local motions or tracking, allowing dynamic changes of the controlled body region.
limitations: Conflicting commands on mechanically coupled parts can fail, such as different leg tasks. Partial tracking inherits the kinematic generator’s semantic errors. Evaluation in a particular simulator and selected reference combinations does not establish robust manipulation or real-hardware transfer.
method: MaskAdapt learns an adversarial base policy with observation masks and a mask-invariant regularizer, then trains a residual adaptation policy controlling selected parts. The base preserves non-adapted behavior while residual rewards teach new local motions or tracking, allowing dynamic changes of the controlled body region.
conditions: Proprioception, body-part masks, and task/reference signals; text-driven examples rely on a pretrained kinematic generator supplying partial trajectories. The simulated character has 22 bodies and 63 degrees of freedom, so this is embodied policy adaptation rather than unrestricted body-motion decoding.
data_split: Base motions come from LAFAN1, composition clips from AMASS, and partial-tracking trajectories from a BABEL-trained generator. No percentage train/validation/test split is reported for a compositional dataset. Three specified composition cases and task-specific simulations form the principal evaluation.
metrics: Normalized Shannon entropy of reference-frame visitation measures behavioral coverage, separately for adapted and preserved parts. Location/strike/heading success rates assess goals; tracking and pose errors assess partial imitation. These metrics are not equivalent to held-out semantic-combination accuracy.
evaluation: Tables 1–2 compare AMP/base regularization and three composition cases; Table 3 compares goal tasks with AdaptNet/CML; Table 4 evaluates partial tracking. Composition collects 1,000 frames in ten parallel environments, with separate text-conditioned tracking trials and qualitative mask switches.
evidence_locator: §3 base/residual policy and mask invariance; §§4.1–4.3, Tables 1–4 and Figures 5–8; conclusion limitations and supplementary task settings.

title: Learning Multi-Modal Whole-Body Control for Real-World Humanoid Robots
summary: Masked Humanoid Controller learns one policy to track selectively masked motion directives while obeying locomotion commands. A staged curriculum, offset-aware future directives, motion/style rewards, perturbations, and dynamics randomization teach compatibility between whole-body mimicry, upper-body motion, standing, and joystick walking.
limitations: The chosen motion corpus avoids the most aggressive behaviors and robot morphology restricts transfer. Inconsistent directives and limited mask patterns remain open issues. Real-world task demonstrations do not establish text-semantic composition or arbitrary object interaction.
method: Masked Humanoid Controller learns one policy to track selectively masked motion directives while obeying locomotion commands. A staged curriculum, offset-aware future directives, motion/style rewards, perturbations, and dynamics randomization teach compatibility between whole-body mimicry, upper-body motion, standing, and joystick walking.
conditions: Motion target trajectories with body-part masks, root velocity/turn commands, standing indicator, and robot proprioception. Outputs are joint PD setpoints for Digit. The policy combines control modalities; a natural-language generator is not part of the principal system.
data_split: Uses 75 retargeted trajectories partitioned into setA (20), setB (20), and setC (35), with increasing difficulty and mixed AMASS/animation/optimized/video sources. Models trained on A, AB, and ABC are evaluated across sets; this is not a random percentage subject split.
metrics: Mean End-Effector Position Error (EMEPE) measures specified limb positions relative to the torso; root drift measures global locomotion/standing error; failure percentage measures terminated episodes. Perturbation tests apply 50N/100N torso forces; hardware tests omit root error when global localization is unavailable.
evaluation: Tables 2–5 compare walking/standing, offset-aware baselines, dataset scaling, and curriculum ablations. Full/partial mimicry follows each directive once, while locomotion episodes last ten seconds. Real Digit tests evaluate the 20 setA motions and demonstrate upper-body tracking with locomotion.
evidence_locator: Method sections Motion Directives/Curriculum/Reward Design; Motion Directive Dataset (20/20/35), Experimental Setup and Metrics, Tables 2–5; Real-World Experiments and conclusion.

title: Universal Humanoid Motion Representations for Physics-Based Control
summary: PULSE first trains a stronger PHC+ motion imitator, then distills its motor knowledge into a variational bottleneck with a proprioception-conditioned latent prior. A frozen decoder maps latent actions into motor controls, while new high-level RL policies learn downstream tasks in that reusable action space.
limitations: Simulator rewards and cleaned reference coverage influence results. Reusing a latent action space still requires task-policy training and does not imply arbitrary semantic combinations. Controller tracking is insufficient to assess detailed object grasping, tactile realism, or real humanoid deployment.
method: PULSE first trains a stronger PHC+ motion imitator, then distills its motor knowledge into a variational bottleneck with a proprioception-conditioned latent prior. A frozen decoder maps latent actions into motor controls, while new high-level RL policies learn downstream tasks in that reusable action space.
conditions: Robot/humanoid proprioception and task goals, including reference poses, VR controller positions, target speed, reaching/striking, or terrain context. A task-specific high-level policy is trained for each downstream problem; this is not zero-shot natural-language skill composition.
data_split: Cleaned AMASS contains 11,313 training and 138 test sequences after removing unsuitable artifacts. The split is explicitly sequence-based in reported counts; real VR data add 14 trajectories. Downstream RL tasks use simulator goal distributions rather than a common held-out text-motion partition.
metrics: Success requires average per-joint tracking distance below 0.5m throughout the reference. Global/root-relative MPJPE, velocity error, and acceleration error measure imitation; VR uses three-controller tracking error when full-body truth is unavailable. Normalized undiscounted return evaluates generative downstream tasks.
evaluation: Table 1 compares PHC/PHC+/PULSE imitation; Table 2 compares VR tracking against ASE/CALM variants; task learning curves test reach, speed, strike, and terrain. Representation/prior ablations examine coverage and control benefits, while failure recovery is part of the imitator.
evidence_locator: §§4.1–4.3 (PHC+, variational distillation, downstream RL), §5 metrics/experiments, Tables 1–2; appendix B.1 (cleaning/counts), B.2 (control).

title: DeepMimic: Example-Guided Deep Reinforcement Learning of Physics-Based Character Skills
summary: DeepMimic trains physics-based policies with PPO to maximize imitation and task rewards. Pose, joint velocity, end-effector, and center-of-mass terms reproduce reference clips; reference-state initialization and early termination improve difficult-skill learning. Multi-clip objectives and policy composition enable broader behavioral repertoires.
limitations: Learned skills depend on reference coverage, simulator fidelity, and reward design; multi-clip capabilities do not prove unseen linguistic task combinations. Simulated Atlas morphology is not hardware deployment. Contact emerging in simulation should not be generalized to dexterous human-object manipulation.
method: DeepMimic trains physics-based policies with PPO to maximize imitation and task rewards. Pose, joint velocity, end-effector, and center-of-mass terms reproduce reference clips; reference-state initialization and early termination improve difficult-skill learning. Multi-clip objectives and policy composition enable broader behavioral repertoires.
conditions: Proprioception, reference phase, and optional task goals or terrain observations. Policies output PD targets for articulated simulated characters, including humanoid, Atlas, T-Rex, and dragon. Explicit reference skills and rewards supply the behavior specification rather than free-form text.
data_split: Not applicable as a conventional supervised train/test dataset split. Policies learn designated reference clips and are evaluated on simulator episodes, task goals, perturbations, and terrain. Table 2 lists skill-specific training samples and performance rather than held-out human/recording proportions.
metrics: Normalized episode return measures achievement of imitation/task rewards relative to possible reward bounds. Training-sample counts and learning curves measure efficiency; task trials assess recovery, terrain traversal, target accuracy, and skill composition. These rewards are method-specific and not general motion-distribution scores.
evaluation: Section 6/Table 2 evaluate acrobatic and locomotion skills across characters, while subsequent experiments add task adaptation, perturbation recovery, multi-skill agents, and obstacle traversal. Ablations assess reference initialization and termination; qualitative videos support motion-quality judgments.
evidence_locator: §4 rewards/training, §5 environments/characters, §6 and Table 2 (normalized returns and samples), task adaptation, robustness, multi-skill and ablation subsections.

title: BeyondMimic: From Motion Tracking to Versatile Humanoid Control via Guided Diffusion
summary: BeyondMimic trains robust whole-body tracking policies with adaptive motion sampling and sim-to-real randomization, distills their action trajectories into latent diffusion, and guides diffusion at inference with differentiable task costs. Combining costs enables fresh waypoint, joystick, obstacle, and motion-inpainting objectives without task-specific RL retraining.
limitations: Guidance relies on tractable differentiable objectives and remains sensitive to data support and modeling errors. Successful G1 demonstrations are task-specific, not proof of arbitrary manipulation or semantic language composition. Per-motion tracking and distilled general policies should be distinguished in comparisons.
method: BeyondMimic trains robust whole-body tracking policies with adaptive motion sampling and sim-to-real randomization, distills their action trajectories into latent diffusion, and guides diffusion at inference with differentiable task costs. Combining costs enables fresh waypoint, joystick, obstacle, and motion-inpainting objectives without task-specific RL retraining.
conditions: Robot proprioception and task commands, optional keyframes, waypoints, or scene obstacles; low-level latent actions generate joint commands. Scene-aware guidance uses environmental localization information, whereas many tracking demonstrations run onboard without external motion capture.
data_split: Reference motions are drawn from several prior collections, Unitree-retargeted LAFAN1, and animation packs; supplementary Table S8 lists validated motions. No standard human/recording-disjoint train/validation/test ratio is reported. Unseen tasks mean new test-time cost objectives, not necessarily unseen source motion categories.
metrics: Tracking errors measure global/local pose accuracy; motion completion without falling defines cartwheel transfer success. Learning curves and failure rates assess adaptive sampling; task-specific navigation/command errors and hardware rollouts assess guided control. Latency and deployment constraints affect practical feasibility.
evaluation: The Results section separates scalable tracking from inference-time skill repurposing. Adaptive-sampling ablations compare difficult segments, latent-diffusion ablations test cartwheel sim-to-sim transfer, and real Unitree G1 examples demonstrate selected skills, transitions, and guided tasks.
evidence_locator: Results: Scalable Learning, Versatile Control, Adaptive Sampling and Latent Diffusion ablations; Methods motion tracking/diffusion guidance; supplementary S2/Table S8 and deployment settings.

title: CFGComposer: Compositional Audio-Text-to-Motion Generation via Copula Score Correction
summary: CFGComposer combines frozen audio-to-motion and text-to-motion diffusion experts, deriving a missing cross-modal score term relative to naive product-of-experts fusion. A jointly trained audio-text denoiser estimates an epsilon-space correction; an inference weight interpolates or amplifies that correction over the composed expert prediction.
limitations: The method is not training-free: a joint model learns the correction. At scale one its defined correction returns the joint prediction algebraically; probabilistic interpretation does not independently prove estimator accuracy. Sparse paired data, validation-only reporting, and whole-body captions limit generalization claims.
method: CFGComposer combines frozen audio-to-motion and text-to-motion diffusion experts, deriving a missing cross-modal score term relative to naive product-of-experts fusion. A jointly trained audio-text denoiser estimates an epsilon-space correction; an inference weight interpolates or amplifies that correction over the composed expert prediction.
conditions: Speech audio encoded with Whisper, a gesture caption, and a framewise gesture-window mask. Five-second clips contain 300 frames and 60 robot joints after G1/BrainCo retargeting. Specified timing is an input, not automatically inferred from unrestricted speech semantics.
data_split: BEAT-derived annotated clips yield 775 training and 195 validation examples after five temporal-offset augmentations per annotation. No separately described held-out test set or speaker/annotation-group split is given in the inspected setup; correlation between offset variants therefore needs checking before reuse.
metrics: G-MSE measures joint error in gesture windows, F-MSE full-clip error, BA audio/motion beat alignment, SRGR semantics-weighted keypoint recall, FID feature-distribution mismatch, and DIV variation. Blind human comparisons assess naturalness, semantic accuracy, beat matching, and diversity.
evaluation: Table I compares prior AT2M systems; ablations compare naive PoE, finetuning, mixed-data training, and correction-scale sweeps. The operating scale 0.7 is selected using semantic fidelity. A real G1 demonstration supplements automatic and preference evaluation.
evidence_locator: §III inputs, §IV score derivation, §V/Algorithms 1–2 training/inference, §VI.A (775/195 clips), Table I, §VI.C scale ablations and deployment.

title: EDGE: Editable Dance Generation From Music
summary: EDGE trains a music-conditioned diffusion Transformer with Jukebox audio features and geometric/foot-contact losses. Diffusion inpainting enforces selected joints or frames, while overlapping conditioned windows enable long dance synthesis and editable transitions without retraining separate editing models.
limitations: Contact-aware losses and PFC are kinematic proxies, not physics-simulator or force validation. Window stitching does not guarantee global choreographic semantics. Dance-domain training and audio transfer cannot establish general text composition, detailed hands, or scene/object interaction.
method: EDGE trains a music-conditioned diffusion Transformer with Jukebox audio features and geometric/foot-contact losses. Diffusion inpainting enforces selected joints or frames, while overlapping conditioned windows enable long dance synthesis and editable transitions without retraining separate editing models.
conditions: Music features, requested motion duration, and optional temporal or jointwise constraints. Supplied poses/joints are preserved during denoising; long sequences concatenate overlapping windows. Music-conditioned dance differs from text-ordered locomotion followed by object manipulation.
data_split: Uses the original AIST++ train/test split, with training examples cut into five-second clips at 30 fps. Exact split counts/proportions are not restated in the main experimental setup. Additional in-the-wild music tests probe audio transfer rather than held-out human-object interaction.
metrics: Kinetic/geometric feature distances measure diversity; beat alignment measures correspondence between music and motion events. Physical Foot Contact (PFC) evaluates foot/contact plausibility from motion signals. Pairwise human judgments yield Elo ratings and win rates with confidence intervals.
evaluation: Table 1 compares FACT, Bailando, and guidance variants; Table 2 tests in-the-wild music and Jukebox-feature ablations. Examples demonstrate joint constraints, in-betweening, and long generation. The paper questions whether standard feature FID reliably matches perceived dance quality.
evidence_locator: §3 diffusion/audio/geometric losses and editing (Figure 3), §4 experimental protocol and Tables 1–2, Equation 10 PFC; appendix A human study.

title: Human Motion Video Generation: A Survey
summary: This narrative survey organizes more than 200 human-motion-video papers around input, motion planning, video generation, refinement, and output. It separates vision-, text-, and audio-driven tasks, compares representative architectures, discusses language-model-assisted planning, and catalogs datasets and evaluation practices.
limitations: Coverage is scoped to video synthesis and reflects the reviewed publication window. Photorealism, identity preservation, or plausible rendered movement cannot establish recoverable metric 3D motion, collision-free contact, or executable humanoid control. Cross-paper scores use incompatible data and metrics.
method: This narrative survey organizes more than 200 human-motion-video papers around input, motion planning, video generation, refinement, and output.
